# Write a script rule

You end with a script rule (lawcheck docs concepts) that finds the calls of `fetch()` outside the api layer. The rule calls code from a helper module that other rules can import. At first, its finding is an error. A later step makes it a warning.

The outputs below come from a repository with three files under `src/`:

- `src/api/orders.ts` calls `fetch()`;
- the second line of `src/core/price.ts` calls `fetch()` too;
- `src/core/tax.ts` makes no such call.

Step 13 adds a fourth file.

The law gives `src/**/*.ts` the type `source`. Its subtypes are `api` for `src/api/` and `core` for `src/core/` (Types for an existing project (lawcheck docs types-for-a-project)).

## 1. Add the rule to the law

Give the rule an entry under `rules`, with its `why`. List the rule on the type whose files it judges:

```yaml
lawcheck: 0.1.0

rules:
  no-fetch:
    why: Only the api layer talks to the network.

types:
  source:
    about: Everything that ships.
    paths: ["src/**/*.ts"]
    types:
      api:
        about: The HTTP handlers.
        paths: ["src/api/**"]
      core:
        about: The business logic.
        paths: ["src/core/**"]
        rules: [no-fetch]
```

## 2. Write a helper the rules share

Lawcheck reads no file below `.lawcheck/rules/lib/` as a rule. Every rule may import such a file. Write `.lawcheck/rules/lib/lines.mjs`:

```js
export function linesMatching(files, pattern, message) {
  const findings = [];
  for (const file of files) {
    file.lines.forEach((text, index) => {
      if (pattern.test(text)) findings.push({ line: index + 1, message });
    });
  }
  return findings;
}
```

## 3. Write the rule

The file of the rule is `.lawcheck/rules/no-fetch.mjs`, as the name of a rule file is the id of its rule. It exports `check`. Lawcheck calls that function with the files of the rule. The function returns a list of findings:

```js
import { linesMatching } from './lib/lines.mjs';

export function check({ files }) {
  return linesMatching(files, /\bfetch\(/, 'calls fetch outside the api layer');
}
```

A second rule imports `./lib/lines.mjs` in the same way. Script rules (lawcheck docs script-rules) says what `check` receives and what a finding holds.

## 4. See the files the rule binds

A rule binds (lawcheck docs concepts) the files of the types that list it.

```text
$ lawcheck explain --rule no-fetch
```

```output
rule no-fetch  script  enforced
  why:  Only the api layer talks to the network.
  file:  .lawcheck/rules/no-fetch.mjs
  on types:  core
  binds:  2 files
    src/core/price.ts
    src/core/tax.ts
```

## 5. Try the rule

Without a path, `lawcheck try` runs a script rule on every file it binds: here, the two files of `core`. A rule that no type lists binds no file. For such a rule, `try` needs a path. Without a path, `try` stops with the error `usage` (lawcheck docs codes) before it runs the rule. Run it without a path:

```text
$ lawcheck try no-fetch
```

```output
lawcheck: try no-fetch (script rule, enforced)  1 finding in 1 of 2 files

src/core/price.ts:2  error[no-fetch]  calls fetch outside the api layer
  why:  Only the api layer talks to the network.
```

`src/api/orders.ts` calls `fetch()` too. It gets no finding, since `api` does not list the rule.

## 6. Check the code

```text
$ lawcheck check src
```

```output
lawcheck: FAIL  1 error in 3 named files

src/core/price.ts:2  error[no-fetch]  calls fetch outside the api layer
  why:  Only the api layer talks to the network.

next: fix src/core/price.ts:2
```

The finding of an enforced rule is an error. `check` exits 1.

## 7. Make the rule advisory

Give the rule `status: advisory` in its entry:

```yaml
rules:
  no-fetch:
    why: Only the api layer talks to the network.
    status: advisory
```

## 8. Check the code again

```text
$ lawcheck check src
```

```output
lawcheck: PASS  1 warning in 3 named files

src/core/price.ts:2  warning[no-fetch]  calls fetch outside the api layer
  why:  Only the api layer talks to the network.
```

The findings of an advisory rule are warnings. `check` exits 0. Without the `status` line, the rule is enforced again.

## 9. Put a typo in the helper

To see a broken rule, write `line` in place of `lines` in the fourth line of `.lawcheck/rules/lib/lines.mjs`:

```js
    file.line.forEach((text, index) => {
```

## 10. Try the broken rule

```text
$ lawcheck try no-fetch
```

```output
lawcheck: ERROR  1 error

.lawcheck/rules/no-fetch.mjs  error[rule-crashed]  throws on src/core/price.ts: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'forEach')
  why:  a broken rule says nothing about the code

next: fix .lawcheck/rules/no-fetch.mjs, then run lawcheck try again
```

The error names the file of the rule, though the line that throws is in the helper. Its message names `src/core/price.ts` and the error that the rule threw. `try` and `check` exit 2, because a broken rule says nothing about the code (rule-crashed (lawcheck docs codes)).

## 11. Fix the helper

Write `lines` again:

```js
    file.lines.forEach((text, index) => {
```

## 12. Try the rule again

```text
$ lawcheck try no-fetch
```

```output
lawcheck: try no-fetch (script rule, advisory)  1 finding in 1 of 2 files

src/core/price.ts:2  warning[no-fetch]  calls fetch outside the api layer
  why:  Only the api layer talks to the network.
```

`try` exits 1 on a finding, an advisory one included.

## 13. Read the syntax tree

The rule reads lines, so it also reports `fetch(` in a comment or a string. Add `src/core/cart.ts`, whose first line is a comment:

```ts
// Orders reach the network through fetch() in src/api, never here.
export async function total() {
  return (await fetch('/cart')).json();
}
```

The rule of step 3 reports line 1 and line 3 of this file. Write `.lawcheck/rules/no-fetch.mjs` again. This time it reads the syntax tree (lawcheck docs script-rules) of the file and reports only a call whose function is `fetch`:

```js
export async function check({ files: [file] }) {
  const { root } = await file.tree();
  if (root === null) return [];
  const findings = [];
  const stack = [root];
  while (stack.length > 0) {
    const node = stack.pop();
    const callee = node.type === 'call_expression' ? node.children.find((child) => child.field === 'function') : undefined;
    if (callee && file.text.slice(callee.start, callee.end) === 'fetch') findings.push({ line: node.line, message: 'calls fetch outside the api layer' });
    stack.push(...node.children);
  }
  return findings;
}
```

A comment is a node of type `comment`, so the rule never reports it. A file with no tree, such as a file in a language Lawcheck does not read, gets no finding. The rule no longer imports `./lib/lines.mjs`, and another rule can still import it.

```text
$ lawcheck try no-fetch
```

```output
lawcheck: try no-fetch (script rule, advisory)  2 findings in 2 of 3 files

src/core/cart.ts:3  warning[no-fetch]  calls fetch outside the api layer
  why:  Only the api layer talks to the network.
src/core/price.ts:2  warning[no-fetch]  calls fetch outside the api layer
```

The finding in `src/core/cart.ts` is on line 3, the call. Line 1, the comment, has none.

## If it goes wrong

- Lawcheck prints `rule-crashed`, and the message says the rule cannot find a package: the rule imports a package that no `node_modules` below the root (lawcheck docs concepts) of the law holds. Lawcheck lets a rule read files only below the root and in the folder of Lawcheck. A rule cannot load a package from a `node_modules` above the root, where a monorepo can keep it. Install the package below the root, or write the code in `.lawcheck/rules/lib/`.
- Lawcheck prints `rule-crashed`, and the message says the rule passes 30 seconds on a file: one call of `check` on one file took longer than 30 seconds. The load of the rule module has its own limit of 30 seconds. Make the rule do less work per file.
- Lawcheck prints `rules-too-slow`: the script rules of one run took over 600 seconds together. List the rule on fewer types, or narrow their paths.
- Lawcheck prints `rule-crashed` with `writes` or `reads` and a path: the rule wrote a file, or read outside the root. Lawcheck stopped it. A rule may write no file. It may read no file outside the root and the folder of Lawcheck.
- The rule finds nothing in a file where you expected a finding: the file has no type that lists the rule. `lawcheck explain <path>` shows its rules.
- `lawcheck try no-fetch` stops with `usage` (lawcheck docs codes): no file has a type that lists the rule. Name the files, or list the rule on a type as in [Add the rule to the law](#_1-add-the-rule-to-the-law).
- `lawcheck check` without a path passes on code that breaks a new rule: without a path or `--full`, it judges the changed files only. `lawcheck check --full` lists the rest as debt.

Next: Write a reviewer rule (lawcheck docs write-a-reviewer-rule)
# Script rules

A to-do comment without an issue number stays in the code for years. A script rule (lawcheck docs concepts) finds it. The rule is an ES module in `.lawcheck/rules/<id>.mjs` that exports a function `check`. The law names the rule in `.lawcheck/law.yaml`, with its `why` and its `status` (`lawcheck docs law` has the keys). The folder that holds `.lawcheck/` is the root of the law (lawcheck docs concepts). This page calls it the root for short. Every path in the tables below starts there.

```js
export function check({ files }) {
  const findings = [];
  for (const file of files) {
    file.lines.forEach((text, index) => {
      if (text.includes('TODO') && !/#\d/.test(text)) findings.push({ line: index + 1, message: 'TODO without an issue number' });
    });
  }
  return findings;
}
```

## The argument of check

`check` gets one object with the keys `files` and `repo`.

| Key | Value |
|---|---|
| `files` | a list that holds the one file of the call |
| `path` | the file's path from the root, as Lawcheck prints it |
| `type` | the file's type id; under `lawcheck try`, null for a file with no type |
| `text` | the file's text |
| `lines` | the text split at `\n` and `\r\n` |
| `tree()` | a promise of the file's [syntax tree](#the-syntax-tree) |
| `uses()` | a promise of the file's [uses](#the-uses), the ones that `may_use` judges |
| `repo.filesOf(typeId)` | the sorted paths of every file of that type and its subtypes, at once; an unknown id throws |

Lawcheck reads the tree and the uses only when the rule calls `tree()` or `uses()`. A rule that calls neither makes Lawcheck parse nothing for it. A second call in the same call of `check` gives the same promise. On a file kept from an earlier call, `tree()` rejects with `tree() was called after its call of check ended`, and `uses()` with the same message about `uses()`.

In `path`, Lawcheck writes a backslash, a line feed, a carriage return and a byte that is not UTF-8 as `\\`, `\n`, `\r` and `\xHH`. Such a `path` no longer names the file on disk, so read the file's text from `text`. A final line end adds no empty line to `lines`. For an empty file, `lines` is an empty list.

## The syntax tree

This rule finds a call of `eval`. A string or a comment that holds `eval(x)` is no call, so the rule does not report it.

```js
export async function check({ files: [file] }) {
  const { root } = await file.tree();
  if (root === null) return [];
  const findings = [];
  const stack = [root];
  while (stack.length > 0) {
    const node = stack.pop();
    const callee = node.type === 'call_expression' ? node.children.find((child) => child.field === 'function') : undefined;
    if (callee && file.text.slice(callee.start, callee.end) === 'eval') findings.push({ line: node.line, message: 'eval runs text as code' });
    stack.push(...node.children);
  }
  return findings;
}
```

`await file.tree()` gives an object with three keys:

| Key | Value |
|---|---|
| `language` | the language the reader parsed, such as `typescript` or `tsx`; null for a file with no reader |
| `root` | the root node, or null when the tree is absent |
| `absent` | null, or why the tree is absent |

Each node has these keys:

| Key | Value |
|---|---|
| `type` | the node's type in the grammar, such as `call_expression` or `comment` |
| `named` | false for a keyword or a punctuation mark such as `let` or `(`, true for the other nodes |
| `field` | the name its parent gives the node, such as `name` or `body`, or null |
| `start`, `end` | where the node starts and ends in `text`, so `text.slice(node.start, node.end)` is its text |
| `line` | the line of `start`, counted from 1, as in `lines` and in a finding |
| `column` | the column of `start` in its line, counted from 0 in UTF-16 code units, as JavaScript counts a string |
| `children` | the node's children, in the order of the text |

A node of type `ERROR` holds text that the grammar cannot read. Where the text lacks a token, the parser can add a node whose `start` equals its `end`. A Vue or Svelte file gets the tree of its script blocks. Lawcheck parses that file with every character outside the blocks turned into a space, so `start` and `end` still point into `text`.

The tree depends on the file's path and text. A header of C or C++ also depends on the other files of its folder, which decide its language (Languages and uses (lawcheck docs languages)). A plain check and `--full` give a rule the same tree for the same file.

The tree is absent in three cases:

| `absent` | When |
|---|---|
| `no-reader` | no reader reads the file's language (Languages and uses (lawcheck docs languages)), or a Vue or Svelte file has no script block |
| `too-large` | the parsed text holds more than 512 KiB, the limit of a file whose uses are read |
| `reader-failed` | Lawcheck cannot load the grammar of the language, or the parser fails on the file |

An absent tree stops nothing. The rule decides what to report for that file.

### The grammars

The node types and fields come from the grammar of each language. Lawcheck ships the grammars of Runes 1.2.0:

| `language` | Version of the grammar |
|---|---|
| `typescript`, `tsx` | 0.23.2, with four fixes from the grammar's own repository |
| `javascript` | 0.25.0 |
| `python` | 0.25.0 |
| `go` | 0.25.0 |
| `rust` | 0.24.2 |
| `java` | 0.23.5 |
| `kotlin` | 1.1.0 |
| `csharp` | a commit after 0.23.5, not released, that reads C# 14 |
| `c` | 0.24.2 |
| `cpp` | a commit after 0.23.4, not released |
| `php` | a commit after 0.24.2, not released |
| `ruby` | a commit after 0.23.1, not released |

Lawcheck sets the keys of the result and of a node. A version of Lawcheck that changes them says so in the changelog, under "Before you upgrade". The grammar sets the node types, the fields and the nesting. A new version of Lawcheck can take a new Runes with new grammars, and the same code can then give other node types, other fields or other nesting. The changelog names each version of Lawcheck that changes a grammar, and this table shows the grammar versions.

## The uses

`await file.uses()` gives an object with two keys:

| Key | Value |
|---|---|
| `uses` | the uses the reader found, in the order of the file, or null when they are absent |
| `absent` | null, or why the uses are absent: `no-reader`, `too-large` or `reader-failed`, as for the tree |

A Vue or Svelte file with no script block has no uses, so its list is empty, while its tree is absent with `no-reader`.

Each use has `line` and `kind`. These are the same uses that `may_use` judges (Languages and uses (lawcheck docs languages)):

| `kind` | Other keys | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `file` | `file`, `type` | the use reaches a file of the repository; `file` is that file's path, written as `path` is, and `type` its type id, or null for a file with no type |
| `outside` | none | the use leaves the repository, such as an import of a package |
| `ambiguous` | `what`, `candidates` | the use could name several files; `candidates` lists them |
| `none` | `what`, `reason`, `candidates` | the readers found no file; `reason` is `unfollowed`, `unowned` or null, as in Unresolved uses (lawcheck docs languages) |

The list holds what `may_use` skips: a use of the file itself, and a use of a binary file.

The first call of `uses()` by a rule reads, at once, the uses of every file the rule judges in that run. Lawcheck reads the uses of each file once in a run, so a file whose uses another rule already asked for is not read again, and every rule gets the same answer for it. A file of Java, Kotlin, C#, Ruby or Rust needs the declarations of every file of its language, so that first call can take seconds in a large repository. When the reader fails on a file the rule judges, that file gets `reader-failed`, and Lawcheck reads the other files again without it. A failure on anything else gives `reader-failed` to every file that depends on it. A grammar that does not load fails every file of its language. A file of Java, Kotlin, C#, Ruby or Rust that Lawcheck reads only for what it declares fails every file of its language, and Java and Kotlin count as one language here. The uses of a file do not depend on the other files of the run, so a plain check and `--full` give a rule the same uses.

## The return value

`check` returns a list of findings (lawcheck docs concepts), or a promise of one. A finding has these fields:

- `message` is a non-empty string of at most 4,096 characters. Lawcheck turns a line break in it into a space.
- `line` is optional. Its value is an integer from 1 to the number of lines of the file. A finding without `line`, or with a `line` of `null`, is about the whole file. A `line` that is any other value than an integer in that range, such as a string like `'2'`, a bigint or `1.5`, makes the rule `rule-crashed`, with a message that names the value.
- `file` is optional. Its one allowed value is the `path` of the call.

Lawcheck ignores other fields. A rule that returns an empty list reports no finding. All the rules of one run may return 200,000 findings together, with 16 MiB of messages. A run past either limit stops with `too-many-findings`. The error names each rule with the number of findings it returned.

## Calls

Lawcheck calls `check` once for each file of the run whose type, or a type above it, lists the rule. It makes the calls in path order, one call at a time. A plain `lawcheck check` (lawcheck docs concepts) passes the rule the files of the change (lawcheck docs concepts). With `--full`, Lawcheck passes it every file that the rule binds, changed or not. Keep nothing between calls in a rule. A rule that counts the files it has seen reaches one count in a plain check and another with `--full`, so its findings differ between the two.

Lawcheck does not load a rule that has no file to judge in the run.

## The runner

Lawcheck runs each script rule in a Node process of its own. This page calls that process the rule runner. Lawcheck's own folder is the folder where the `lawcheck` package is installed. The rule runner starts in this state:

- Node's flag `--permission` limits its reads to the root and to Lawcheck's own folder;
- `process.env` is empty, because the rule runner gets none of the caller's variables;
- its working directory is the root.

Lawcheck writes what the rule prints, on either stream, to its own standard error.

A rule has 30 seconds to load and 30 seconds for each call. A rule that takes longer is `rule-crashed`. All script rules of one run have 600 seconds together. The time Lawcheck takes to read a tree or the uses counts toward the 600 seconds of the run, and not toward the 30 seconds of any call. A rule that asks while Lawcheck reads for another rule does not lose that time either. A run that goes past the 600 seconds stops with `rules-too-slow`. Lawcheck reports that code at the file that each unfinished rule was judging.

The rule runner refuses these actions:

- writing, renaming or deleting a file, or making a directory, through `node:fs`;
- reading through `node:fs` outside the root and Lawcheck's folder;
- starting a child process or a worker thread;
- loading a native add-on or WASI;
- using the network: opening a connection, listening on a port, sending over UDP or looking up a name in DNS. The rule runner closes `node:net`, `node:dgram`, `node:dns` and the globals `fetch` and `WebSocket` before the rule loads. `node:http`, `node:https` and `node:tls` open their connections through `node:net`, and fail the same way;
- importing `node:sqlite`. Node's permission model is the set of limits that `--permission` turns on. That model leaves `node:sqlite` open, so the rule runner starts Node without that module. No rule can open, attach or write a database through it. In a rule, `process.getBuiltinModule('node:sqlite')` returns `undefined`.

Each refused action throws an error inside the rule. A rule that does not catch that error is `rule-crashed`. The message of `rule-crashed` then says what the rule did, such as `reads <path> outside the root and Lawcheck's folder, and a rule may read nothing else`, `writes <path>, and a rule may write no file`, `uses the network, which is closed to script rules` or `imports node:sqlite, and a rule may not`.

A rule may import these modules:

- the `node:` built-ins;
- files below the root, such as `.lawcheck/rules/lib/`;
- packages installed in a `node_modules` folder below the root.

A rule fails to load when it imports one of these packages:

- a package in a `node_modules` above the root, as in a monorepo whose law sits in one package;
- a package reached through a symbolic link that leads outside the root.

Install each package the rule needs in a `node_modules` below the root.

The rule runner does not shut a rule off from your machine. A rule can still do these things:

- read every file under the root, `.git/` and ignored files such as `.env` included;
- read any file you can read, through a symbolic link under the root that git does not track;
- read a file elsewhere in the git work tree, through a tracked link. A tracked link that leads outside the work tree stops the run with `link-outside-root` before any rule starts;
- put what it read into its messages. Lawcheck prints those messages, and a CI job keeps them in its log.

A rule file is code of the repository. It runs with your rights, as the tests do. Run `lawcheck check` and `lawcheck try` only where you would run the tests of the change.

Lawcheck stops the run with `path-unsupported` when the path of the root, or of Lawcheck's own folder, holds a `*`. Node's permission model reads that `*` as a wildcard, which would let a rule read the folders beside the root. Outside Windows, a backslash in either path stops the run too, because the rule runner cannot load a rule from such a path.

## rule-crashed

Lawcheck reports `rule-crashed` and exits with code 2 when the rule:

- does not load, or exports no function `check`;
- throws or rejects;
- returns something other than a list of findings as above. A list with a message over 4,096 characters counts as such a return. So does a function, or another value that Lawcheck cannot pass out of the rule's process;
- takes more than 30 seconds to load, or more than 30 seconds for one call;
- ends its process before it answers, or sends a message that Lawcheck did not ask for;
- leaves a promise rejected with no handler, or a timer that throws, while its process runs. The message of `rule-crashed` then names no judged file. A failure during the load adds the words `in its load`. After the last call, Lawcheck waits once, at most 2 seconds, for what the rule left running. A timer counts whether or not the rule unrefs it.

In the other cases, the message of `rule-crashed` names the judged file, or the load. A rule may throw a value with no string form, such as an object with no prototype. The message then holds the error JavaScript gives for it. A proxy whose every trap throws something other than an error raises no such error. For such a value, the message reads `a value with no string form`. Lawcheck names each crashed rule once in a run.

When Node cannot start the rule runner at all, Lawcheck stops with `runner-failed` and names no rule. The message holds Node's own error line. To fix it, reinstall Lawcheck.

## Trying a rule

```text
$ lawcheck try no-todo src/core/tax.ts
$ lawcheck try no-todo
```

With a file named, `lawcheck try` runs the rule on that file. Without one, it runs a script rule on every file whose type, or a type above it, lists the rule. `lawcheck try` records nothing in the repository. `lawcheck docs first-law` shows how to write a rule and try it, step by step.

# Script rules

A to-do comment without an issue number stays in the code for years. A script rule (lawcheck docs concepts) finds it. The rule is an ES module in `.lawcheck/rules/<id>.mjs` that exports a function `check`. The law names the rule in `.lawcheck/law.yaml`, with its `why` and its `status` (`lawcheck docs law` has the keys). The folder that holds `.lawcheck/` is the root of the law (lawcheck docs concepts). This page calls it the root for short. Every path in the tables below starts there.

```js
export function check({ files }) {
  const findings = [];
  for (const file of files) {
    file.lines.forEach((text, index) => {
      if (text.includes('TODO') && !/#\d/.test(text)) findings.push({ line: index + 1, message: 'TODO without an issue number' });
    });
  }
  return findings;
}
```

## The argument of check

`check` gets one object with the keys `files` and `repo`.

| Key | Value |
|---|---|
| `files` | a list that holds the one file of the call |
| `path` | the file's path from the root, as Lawcheck prints it |
| `type` | the file's type id; under `lawcheck try`, null for a file with no type |
| `text` | the file's text |
| `lines` | the text split at `\n` and `\r\n` |
| `tree()` | a promise of the file's [syntax tree](#the-syntax-tree) |
| `uses()` | a promise of the file's [uses](#the-uses), the ones that `may_use` judges |
| `repo.filesOf(typeId)` | the sorted paths of every file of that type and its subtypes, at once; an unknown id throws |

Lawcheck reads the tree and the uses only when the rule calls `tree()` or `uses()`. A rule that calls neither makes Lawcheck parse nothing for it. A second call in the same call of `check` gives the same promise. On a file kept from an earlier call, `tree()` rejects with `tree() was called after its call of check ended`, and `uses()` with the same message about `uses()`.

In `path`, Lawcheck writes a backslash, a line feed, a carriage return and a byte that is not UTF-8 as `\\`, `\n`, `\r` and `\xHH`. Such a `path` no longer names the file on disk, so read the file's text from `text`. A final line end adds no empty line to `lines`. For an empty file, `lines` is an empty list.

## The syntax tree

This rule finds a call of `eval`. A string or a comment that holds `eval(x)` is no call, so the rule does not report it.

```js
export async function check({ files: [file] }) {
  const { root } = await file.tree();
  if (root === null) return [];
  const findings = [];
  const stack = [root];
  while (stack.length > 0) {
    const node = stack.pop();
    const callee = node.type === 'call_expression' ? node.children.find((child) => child.field === 'function') : undefined;
    if (callee && file.text.slice(callee.start, callee.end) === 'eval') findings.push({ line: node.line, message: 'eval runs text as code' });
    stack.push(...node.children);
  }
  return findings;
}
```

`await file.tree()` gives an object with three keys:

| Key | Value |
|---|---|
| `language` | the language the reader parsed, such as `typescript` or `tsx`; null for a file with no reader |
| `root` | the root node, or null when the tree is absent |
| `absent` | null, or why the tree is absent |

Each node has these keys:

| Key | Value |
|---|---|
| `type` | the node's type in the grammar, such as `call_expression` or `comment` |
| `named` | false for a keyword or a punctuation mark such as `let` or `(`, true for the other nodes |
| `field` | the name its parent gives the node, such as `name` or `body`, or null |
| `start`, `end` | where the node starts and ends in `text`, so `text.slice(node.start, node.end)` is its text |
| `line` | the line of `start`, counted from 1, as in `lines` and in a finding |
| `column` | the column of `start` in its line, counted from 0 in UTF-16 code units, as JavaScript counts a string |
| `children` | the node's children, in the order of the text |

A node of type `ERROR` holds text that the grammar cannot read. Where the text lacks a token, the parser can add a node whose `start` equals its `end`. A Vue or Svelte file gets the tree of its script blocks. Lawcheck parses that file with every character outside the blocks turned into a space, so `start` and `end` still point into `text`.

The tree depends on the file's path and text. A header of C or C++ also depends on the other files of its folder, which decide its language (Languages and uses (lawcheck docs languages)). A plain check and `--full` give a rule the same tree for the same file.

The tree is absent in three cases:

| `absent` | When |
|---|---|
| `no-reader` | no reader reads the file's language (Languages and uses (lawcheck docs languages)), or a Vue or Svelte file has no script block |
| `too-large` | the parsed text holds more than 512 KiB, the limit of a file whose uses are read |
| `reader-failed` | Lawcheck cannot load the grammar of the language, or the parser fails on the file |

An absent tree stops nothing. The rule decides what to report for that file.

| `javascript` | 0.25.0 |
| `python` | 0.25.0 |
| `go` | 0.25.0 |
| `rust` | 0.24.2 |
| `java` | 0.23.5 |
| `kotlin` | 1.1.0 |
| `csharp` | a commit after 0.23.5, not released, that reads C# 14 |
| `c` | 0.24.2 |
| `cpp` | a commit after 0.23.4, not released |

| `ruby` | a commit after 0.23.1, not released |

A new version of Lawcheck can take a new Runes with new grammars, and the same code can then give other node types, other fields or other nesting. - reading through `node:fs` outside the root and Lawcheck's folder;
- starting a child process or a worker thread;
- loading a native add-on or WASI;
- using the network: opening a connection, listening on a port, sending over UDP or looking up a name in DNS. The rule runner closes `node:net`, `node:dgram`, `node:dns` and the globals `fetch` and `WebSocket` before the rule loads. `node:http`, `node:https` and `node:tls` open their connections through `node:net`, and fail the same way;
- importing `node:sqlite`. Node's permission model is the set of limits that `--permission` turns on. That model leaves `node:sqlite` open, so the rule runner starts Node without that module. No rule can open, attach or write a database through it. In a rule, `process.getBuiltinModule('node:sqlite')` returns `undefined`.

Each refused action throws an error inside the rule. A rule that does not catch that error is `rule-crashed`. The message of `rule-crashed` then says what the rule did, such as `reads <path> outside the root and Lawcheck's folder, and a rule may read nothing else`, `writes <path>, and a rule may write no file`, `uses the network, which is closed to script rules` or `imports node:sqlite, and a rule may not`.

A rule may import these modules:

- the `node:` built-ins;
- files below the root, such as `.lawcheck/rules/lib/`;
- packages installed in a `node_modules` folder below the root.

A rule fails to load when it imports one of these packages:

- a package in a `node_modules` above the root, as in a monorepo whose law sits in one package;
- a package reached through a symbolic link that leads outside the root.

Install each package the rule needs in a `node_modules` below the root.

The rule runner does not shut a rule off from your machine. A rule can still do these things:

- read every file under the root, `.git/` and ignored files such as `.env` included;
- read any file you can read, through a symbolic link under the root that git does not track;
- read a file elsewhere in the git work tree, through a tracked link. A tracked link that leads outside the work tree stops the run with `link-outside-root` before any rule starts;
- put what it read into its messages. Lawcheck prints those messages, and a CI job keeps them in its log.

A rule file is code of the repository. It runs with your rights, as the tests do. Run `lawcheck check` and `lawcheck try` only where you would run the tests of the change.

Lawcheck stops the run with `path-unsupported` when the path of the root, or of Lawcheck's own folder, holds a `*`. Node's permission model reads that `*` as a wildcard, which would let a rule read the folders beside the root. Outside Windows, a backslash in either path stops the run too, because the rule runner cannot load a rule from such a path.

## rule-crashed

Lawcheck reports `rule-crashed` and exits with code 2 when the rule:

- does not load, or exports no function `check`;
- throws or rejects;
- returns something other than a list of findings as above. A list with a message over 4,096 characters counts as such a return. So does a function, or another value that Lawcheck cannot pass out of the rule's process;
- takes more than 30 seconds to load, or more than 30 seconds for one call;
- ends its process before it answers, or sends a message that Lawcheck did not ask for;
- leaves a promise rejected with no handler, or a timer that throws, while its process runs. The message of `rule-crashed` then names no judged file. A failure during the load adds the words `in its load`. After the last call, Lawcheck waits once, at most 2 seconds, for what the rule left running. A timer counts whether or not the rule unrefs it.

In the other cases, the message of `rule-crashed` names the judged file, or the load. A rule may throw a value with no string form, such as an object with no prototype. The message then holds the error JavaScript gives for it. A proxy whose every trap throws something other than an error raises no such error. For such a value, the message reads `a value with no string form`. Lawcheck names each crashed rule once in a run.

When Node cannot start the rule runner at all, Lawcheck stops with `runner-failed` and names no rule. The message holds Node's own error line. To fix it, reinstall Lawcheck.

## Trying a rule

```text
$ lawcheck try no-todo src/core/tax.ts
$ lawcheck try no-todo
```

With a file named, `lawcheck try` runs the rule on that file. Without one, it runs a script rule on every file whose type, or a type above it, lists the rule. `lawcheck try` records nothing in the repository. `lawcheck docs first-law` shows how to write a rule and try it, step by step.
